      10. The Lebesgue and Riemann integrals#

      The Lebesgue integral of a bounded measurable function on was built from simple functions, while the Riemann integral was built from lower and upper sums over partitions of . In these notes we compare the two constructions. We establish Lebesgue’s criterion, which characterizes the Riemann integrable functions by the size of their set of discontinuities, and we show that the Riemann and Lebesgue integrals agree whenever the former exists.

      The proof expresses the lower Riemann integral of a bounded function as the Lebesgue integral of its lower semicontinuous envelope, and the upper Riemann integral as the Lebesgue integral of its upper semicontinuous envelope. For this purpose we study semicontinuous functions, the envelopes, and an infimal convolution that approximates a lower semicontinuous function from below by Lipschitz functions.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • State Lebesgue’s criterion for Riemann integrability and use it to decide whether a given bounded function is Riemann integrable.

      • Decide whether a function is lower or upper semicontinuous from its level sets.

      • Compute the lower and upper semicontinuous envelopes of a bounded function and identify its discontinuity set as the set where they differ.

      • Approximate a bounded lower semicontinuous function from below by an increasing sequence of Lipschitz functions using an infimal convolution.

      • Prove that the lower and upper Riemann integrals equal the Lebesgue integrals of the lower and upper envelopes.

      Throughout, are real numbers, carries the Lebesgue measure , and for and we write Open and closed sets in are understood relative to the metric .

      10.2 Semicontinuity#

      Continuity of at requires that for near the values lie above and below . A lower Riemann sum records only the infimum of a function on each subinterval, so it is sensitive to the first of these bounds alone, and an upper sum is sensitive to the second alone. Each bound defines a weaker notion than continuity. For example, is not continuous at , since while the values at points of close to equal . The values near nevertheless never fall below , so the lower bound holds at and only the upper bound fails.

The function is lower semicontinuous (LSC) or upper semicontinuous (USC) if it has the corresponding property at every point.

      Proposition 3 (Level-set characterization)#

      For a function , the following assertions hold:

      1. The function is lower semicontinuous if and only if the superlevel set is open for every ; equivalently, if and only if the sublevel set is closed for every .

      2. The function is upper semicontinuous if and only if the sublevel set is open for every ; equivalently, if and only if the superlevel set is closed for every .

      In particular, semicontinuous functions are Borel measurable.
